summary: This version of the Restaurant class accepts an order for a menu item, but only once the kitchen opens at 11:00 AM. Instead of asking the system for the time directly, it reads the time from a Clock object handed to it, which lets a test pretend it is any hour of the day.

lines.text: Clock is Java's replaceable source of the current time; taking one as a dependency is what makes time-based logic testable.

lines.code: private static final LocalTime ORDER_OPEN_TIME = LocalTime.of(11, 0);
lines.text: The opening time is a named constant, so the rule lives in one place rather than as a bare 11 buried inside the method.
Each Restaurant holds on to its own clock for the lifetime of the object, and final guarantees nothing can swap it out later.
The no-argument constructor keeps ordinary code simple: callers who do not care about time control can still write new Restaurant().
This delegates to the other constructor, supplying the real system clock as the default.
This second constructor is the seam a test uses to inject a fake clock fixed at any moment it likes.
A placeholder marking where the spice level method from the earlier exercise still belongs; the new order logic is being added alongside it.
Asking LocalTime.now(clock) rather than LocalTime.now() is the whole trick: the time comes from the injected clock, so it is whatever the test decides.
isBefore compares two times directly, which is clearer and safer than comparing hour and minute numbers by hand.
Returning early keeps the rejection case separate from the success case, so neither branch needs an else.
Once the time check passes, the order is confirmed and the item name is echoed back to the caller.
